soil-water-266.title: Palsas, peat mounds with frozen hearts
soil-water-266.text: A palsa can reach 150 m (490 ft) across and 12 m (39 ft) high, its steep slopes rising above the surrounding peatland. It is a peat mound with a permanently frozen core of peat and mineral soil, typical of peatlands in the zone of discontinuous permafrost. It starts where thin snow lets frost go deeper. An ice lens grows by drawing in water and lifts the surface by frost heave, which lets the cold reach deeper still. Wet or frozen peat lets cold in during winter, while dry surface peat insulates it in summer. So palsas survive where the mean annual temperature is just below freezing. Warming thaws the frozen peat and thickens the {{ref:soil-env-146}}. The peatland grows wetter, and its methane emissions rise.

soil-water-262.title: The Ramsar Convention, a treaty for wetlands
soil-water-262.text: On 2 February 1971, at Ramsar in Iran, countries signed a treaty for the conservation and sustainable use of wetlands. Also called the Convention on Wetlands, it came into force on 21 December 1975 and has 172 parties. Its definition is broad: marsh, fen, peatland or water, natural or artificial, fresh, brackish or salt, including sea no deeper than six metres at low tide. In February 2025 its list held 2,531 Ramsar sites covering over 2.6 million square kilometres. The United Kingdom has the most, 175. Every 2 February is World Wetlands Day, first celebrated in 1997. National follow-through on the treaty is often half-hearted.

soil-fert-198.title: Land loss, when coasts become open water
soil-fert-198.text: The deltas of the Danube, Ganges, Mississippi, Nile and Yellow rivers have all suffered significant land loss. Land loss is the conversion of coastal land to open water by natural processes and human activities. It is broader than coastal erosion. It also covers land lost around estuaries, bays and lakes, and land that vanishes as coastal wetlands subside. Its main causes are coastal erosion, too little sediment supply, subsidence and sea level rise.

soil-water-140.title: The Börde, Germany's black-earth plains
soil-water-140.text: Some of the best soils in Germany lie on its Börden, large, flat, nearly treeless plains of fertile loess. A Börde, a 'fertile plain', is a loess-covered lowland in North Germany, particularly important for arable farming. The Börden stretch from the North German geest to the edge of the Central Uplands. Their loess, laid down mainly by east winds and up to 10 metres thick, evens out the relief. Under a (sub-)oceanic climate it has been largely decalcified and turned to loam. The northern edge of the loess marks a boundary of soil, vegetation and settlement.

soil-water-117.title: Patches, corridors and the landscape mosaic
soil-water-117.text: Seen from above, a landscape is a patchwork. A patch is a relatively uniform area that differs from its surroundings, and patches are a landscape's basic units. They change and fluctuate in a process called patch dynamics. The matrix is the well-connected background they sit in. Corridors are strips of one landscape type that differ from the land on both sides, and linked corridors form a network. Patches, corridors and matrix together make up the mosaic. Connectivity measures how continuous a corridor, network or matrix is. Repeated clearing beyond a critical level breaks continuous cover into isolated patches, so landscapes show a connected and a disconnected phase.

soil-water-118.title: Ecotones, where one community shades into another
soil-water-118.text: A lakeshore is an ecotone, and so is the edge of a field cleared from forest. An ecotone is a transitional zone between two communities, one kind of boundary between landscape patches. Forest giving way to marshland is a classic example, and so is the riparian zone along a stream. An ecotone keeps traits of both neighboring communities and often holds species found in neither. An ecocline is different: a gradual, continuous change in environmental conditions across an ecosystem or community. An ecotope is the smallest ecologically distinct unit used to map and classify landscapes.

soil-water-116.title: Spatial heterogeneity, why unevenness matters
soil-water-116.text: One idea sets landscape ecology apart from other branches of ecology: unevenness. Spatial heterogeneity is the uneven distribution of objects across a landscape, a measure of how its parts differ. Composition is the number and relative abundance of patch types, such as the amount of forest or wetland. Structure adds how those patches are arranged and proportioned. Scale, another main concept, has two meanings: the ratio of map to ground distance, and the extent or resolution of an object or process in space or time. The landscape stability principle holds that structural heterogeneity helps a landscape resist and recover from disturbance.

soil-water-123.title: Blanket bogs, peat draped over the hills
soil-water-123.text: Where rain falls on more than about 235 days a year, peat no longer keeps to the hollows. Blanket bog is peatland that forms where high rainfall and low evapotranspiration let peat cover broad stretches of rolling ground. The rain keeps the surface waterlogged much of the time. Blanket bog is commonest on acidic substrates, but it can form on neutral or even alkaline ones where acidic rainwater outweighs groundwater. It is widespread in the Northern Hemisphere, well studied in Ireland and Scotland, and covers vast areas of North American tundra. It is less developed in the Southern Hemisphere. In parts of Europe its spread is traced to forest clearance by prehistoric peoples.

soil-water-260.title: Constructed wetlands, built to clean dirty water
soil-water-260.text: The East Kolkata Wetlands, a natural system covering 125 square kilometres, treat Kolkata's sewage, and its nutrients feed fish farms and crops. A constructed wetland does that work by design: it is an artificial wetland built to treat sewage, greywater, stormwater runoff or industrial wastewater. Plants, soil and organisms give secondary treatment, removing suspended solids, organic matter, nitrogen and phosphorus through the processes in {{ref:soil-water-127}}. Like natural wetlands, it filters out pathogens and heavy metals, and subsurface-flow designs remove more pathogens than surface ones. Such wetlands are also built to reclaim mined land or to make up for wetlands lost to development.

soil-water-128.title: The services wetlands give for nothing
soil-water-128.text: Replacing what wetlands do would take huge spending on water treatment plants, dams and levees, and many of their services cannot be replaced at all. Wetland ecosystem services are the benefits wetlands give society. Their plants take up and store nutrients from runoff and remove nitrate. They slow the water, so sediment settles out with any heavy metals it carries. Floodplains act as natural reservoirs, spreading floodwater wide to cut its depth and speed, while headwater wetlands slow runoff and snowmelt. Peat-forming wetlands lock away large quantities of carbon that would otherwise reach the atmosphere as CO2.

soil-water-261.title: Wetlands, the largest natural source of methane
soil-water-261.text: Wetlands supply about 20–30% of atmospheric methane, on average about 161 Tg a year, more than any other natural source. Wetland greenhouse gas emissions are the release of methane, nitrous oxide and carbon dioxide from wetland soils. In warm, wet soil, microbes use up oxygen faster than it diffuses in. That creates the anaerobic conditions that the microbes of {{ref:soil-chem-129}} need, and warmth and organic-rich soil boost methane output further. Draining peat exposes carbon stored for thousands of years to air, where it decomposes to CO2. Peatlands cover 3% of land, yet their degradation gives 7% of all CO2 emissions. Some wetlands emit nitrous oxide, with 300 times the warming potential of CO2, though wetlands can also act as greenhouse gas sinks.

soil-water-259.title: Wetland hydrology, the water that makes a wetland
soil-water-259.text: Water, more than anything else, makes a wetland. Wetland hydrology is the flow, storage and chemistry of surface and ground water in a wetland. Water arrives as precipitation, surface water and groundwater. It leaves by evapotranspiration, surface flow, tides and subsurface outflow, and the balance sets the hydroperiod. How long flooding or saturation lasts decides whether a site carries aquatic, marsh or swamp vegetation. Most wetlands are minerotrophic, but ombrotrophic bogs fed only by precipitation have water low in minerals. Fens range from acidic to alkaline and calcium-rich. Wetlands can recharge groundwater when the surrounding water table is low and discharge it when the table is high.

soil-water-135.title: Wetland loss, draining and filling the wet ground
soil-water-135.text: Since 1900 the world's wetlands have shrunk by as much as 50%, and by 90% in some parts of the world. Wetland loss is the draining, filling and conversion of wetlands for agriculture, building and other uses. Europe has likely lost nearly half of its wetlands. More than 50% of its original peat-forming wetland area, once over 300,000 km², has gone to drainage for farming and forestry and to peat harvesting. Settlements built on drained wetlands then face subsidence and rising flood risk, as in the Mississippi delta around New Orleans. Restoration often begins by plugging drainage ditches, removing levees or returning channelized rivers to their natural course so that they flood again.

soil-water-267.title: Peat swamp forests, tropical vaults of carbon
soil-water-267.text: From 1996, Indonesia's Mega Rice Project drained over 1 million hectares of peat forest on Borneo. A peat swamp forest is a tropical moist forest on waterlogged soil. Dead leaves and wood never fully decay there, so a thick layer of acidic peat builds up. It holds far more carbon than forest on mineral soil, among the largest near-surface stores of organic carbon on land. Its peat starts on river-fed deltas, floodplains or oxbow lakes. It then domes up to 4 m on coasts or 18 m inland and turns rain-fed. About 62% of tropical peatland lies in the Indomalayan realm, 80% of it in Indonesia, and 36% lies in Africa's central Congo Basin. Peat fires, drainage and clearing release the stored carbon as CO2.

soil-water-148.title: Shrub swamps, caught between marsh and forest
soil-water-148.text: A shrub swamp is too wet to become swamp forest but too dry or shallow to become marsh. It is a freshwater wetland dominated by shrubs, and some classifications require at least 50% shrub cover and less than 20% tree cover. It often follows floods, cutting, fire or windstorms in a forested swamp, or develops from drained meadows and fens. Its water comes from runoff, streams and rivers and moves in and out through the year. So it is drier than wet meadows or forested swamps, and less water-tolerant plants grow on raised mounds. It typically sits on organic soils such as muck and shallow peat.

soil-water-137.title: Mires, peatlands still at work
soil-water-137.text: A drained peatland may keep its peat, yet it is no longer a mire. A mire is a peatland that is still actively forming peat, and once new peat stops forming, the name no longer fits. There are two types. Bogs rise above their surroundings and are fed only by precipitation. Fens lie on slopes, flats or in depressions, fed by groundwater or the surrounding mineral soil. All mires begin as fens and may become bogs once the peat rises above the land around them. Some swamps are peatlands too, but marshes, whose plants root in mineral soil, generally are not.

soil-phys-162.title: Flarks, the wet hollows between bog ridges
soil-phys-162.text: Many bogs are ribbed, with parallel hollows separated by ridges called strings. Each hollow is a flark, a depression within a bog. Early theories blamed frost heaving, but flarks have since been found where frost heaving does not occur. They are now thought to form when thickening peat slides downslope under its own weight and tears away below obstructions in the terrain beneath. Another theory ties them to patches of the bog that decay faster.

soil-water-152.title: Palustrine wetlands, the inland freshwater catch-all
soil-water-152.text: Marshes, swamps, bogs and fens can all share one label in US wetland classification. A palustrine wetland is any inland, non-tidal wetland whose ocean-derived salts stay below 0.5 parts per thousand. The category takes in inland marshes and swamps as well as bogs, fens, pocosins, tundra and floodplains. It is one of five systems in the Cowardin classification of the US Fish and Wildlife Service, beside marine, estuarine, riverine and lacustrine wetlands. Its vegetation classes are aquatic bed, emergent, scrub-shrub and forested, with woody plants 20 feet tall dividing the last two. Its depressional marshes sit in isolated hollows or on hill slopes, and include vernal pools, playas and prairie potholes.

soil-water-265.title: Floodplain soils, swinging between flood and air
soil-water-265.text: A floodplain's soils change with small steps in elevation, and higher ground farther from the river holds more oxygen. These soils stay aerated between floods. If floodwater stands long enough, though, a saturated soil can run out of oxygen. Its microbes then alternate between aerobic and anaerobic activity, which affects fine-root growth. Floodplains buffer phosphorus strongly, keeping it from reaching the river, especially when they stay connected to the stream. Wet–dry cycles shift redox state, pH and minerals, so formerly flooded soils that dry out hold phosphorus more tightly.

soil-water-120.title: When hydric soil became a legal term
soil-water-120.text: In US federal law, a hydric soil is one that, undrained, is saturated, flooded or ponded long enough in the growing season to turn anaerobic. Such soil supports water-loving vegetation. The term is part of the legal definition of a wetland in the Food Security Act of 1985. The agency in {{ref:soil-hist-050}} uses it to administer that act's 'Swampbuster' provisions. The National Technical Committee for Hydric Soils defines it as soil formed under saturation, flooding or ponding long enough to turn its upper part anaerobic. The Army Corps of Engineers and the Environmental Protection Agency use that definition for Section 404 of the Clean Water Act (1972).

soil-water-142.title: Suffosion, soil that drains away into rock
soil-water-142.text: Most sinkholes do not form when a cave roof gives way. They form by suffosion, the washing of loose soil or sediment down through fissures in the rock beneath. It happens where loose soil, loess or other non-cohesive material lies over limestone with fissures and joints. Rain and surface water carry the material into caves below, leaving a depression at the surface. Suffosion sinkholes are usually linked to karst, though they can form in chalk, gypsum and basalt. Suffosion collapses soil structure, losing both mass and volume as coarse grains lose contact. Suffusion, by contrast, removes fines from between coarse grains that stay in contact, with no change in volume.

soil-water-150.title: String bogs, ribbed peatlands of the cold north
soil-water-150.text: Low ridges 2–3 m wide and under 1 m high run across a string bog at right angles to the flow of water, with wet pools between them. A string bog alternates such slightly raised ridges and islands, carrying woody plants, with flat, wet sedge mats. It lies on gently sloping ground. Its water and its peat, over 1 m thick, are very low in nutrients, because the water drains from other ombrotrophic wetlands. String bogs are a patterned form of blanket bog in periglacial climates. There the {{ref:soil-env-146}} stays frozen for long periods and thaws in spring. They are also called aapa mires, from the Finnish, or Strangmoor, from the German.

soil-water-151.title: Hummocks, small mounds with many origins
soil-water-151.text: A hummock is a small knoll or mound above the surrounding ground, usually under 15 metres high and found in groups or fields. Hummocks form in several ways. In raised bogs such as string bogs, they are low ridges of drier peat moss alternating with shallow wet hollows called flarks. Swamp hummocks usually start as moss-covered fallen trunks or branches rising above the swamp floor. Earth hummocks form in permafrost and seasonally frozen ground, usually in moist, fine-grained soils of low relief, and differential frost heave is the most widely accepted explanation. Inside, the profile is often churned and streaked with organic matter to about the hummock's own height, a form of cryoturbation.

soil-water-133.title: Mima mounds, an unsolved puzzle in the grass
soil-water-133.text: Mima mounds can stud the ground at more than 50 per hectare. They are low, flattened, circular to oval natural mounds of loose, unlayered, often gravelly sediment that form an overthickened A horizon. They span 3 m to more than 50 m across and stand 30 cm to over 2 m high. How they form is still disputed, and no one has shown that all such mounds share one cause. Proposed origins include burrowing pocket gophers, wind-blown sediment caught around plants, earthquake shaking, and shrink–swell clays as in gilgai. Tracer studies showed gophers pushing soil toward mound centres, though they may only maintain existing mounds. In California they sit on stable landforms over 100,000 years old, where a claypan or duripan perches water into vernal pools between them.

soil-water-141.title: Soil-surface roughness, from grains to hillsides
soil-water-141.text: Rain usually smooths a rough soil surface, but on a smooth one it can do the opposite. Soil-surface roughness is the vertical variation in the micro- and macro-relief of a soil surface, together with its statistical distribution. Four classes are recognized by vertical scale. Grain-to-aggregate microrelief spans 0.053–2.0 mm, clods 2–100 mm, and roughness oriented by cultivation 100–300 mm. The fourth is macro-scale topographic curvature. The first two make up microroughness, which rainfall changes over single events and {{ref:soil-agri-095}} over seasons. It is usually measured as Random Roughness, the standard deviation of surface heights about the mean, corrected for slope and for the plow's effects. On surfaces with an initial microroughness of about 0–5 mm, rainfall can raise it considerably.

reviews.soils-in-the-landscape: Water ties this chapter together. Where saturation lasts, soils turn anaerobic and hydric, decay slows, and peat builds up in bogs and fens until peatlands hold between 500 and 700 billion tonnes of carbon. Whether a wetland is fed by rain or by groundwater that has passed through rock sets its pH and nutrients, from acidic bogs to rich fens over limestone. Beside rivers, floods lay down fertile floodplain soils, while riparian strips and marshes trap sediment and strip nitrate from runoff. Drainage undoes this work: drained peat decomposes to CO2, polders sink, and wetlands have shrunk by as much as 50% since 1900.
